prompt: Which signature does `go test -bench` run as a benchmark?
hint: Same rules as a test, with a different prefix and parameter.

choices.why: The prefix is `Benchmark`, in full.
A benchmark takes a `*testing.B`; with a `*testing.T` the go command reports a malformed name.
Right.
A `Test` prefix makes it a test, and a test takes a `*testing.T`.

prompt: `BenchmarkTop` calls `Count` once before its `for b.Loop()`. What does its result measure?

choices.why: Right: the setup before the loop is not timed.
Nothing is divided by two; `Count` runs once, outside the timed loop.

choices.text: `Count` alone, since it is the slower of the two
choices.why: Speed does not decide what is timed; position relative to the loop does.

choices.text: The time it takes to build `sample`
choices.why: `sample` is built at package level, before any benchmark.

prompt: Why does the lesson run benchmarks with `-run '^$'`?

choices.text: It makes the benchmarks run in alphabetical order
choices.why: `-run` selects tests; it says nothing about benchmark order.
Benchmarks are selected by `-bench`.

choices.text: It turns on the memory columns
choices.why: That is `-benchmem`.

choices.text: It matches no test name, so no test runs first
choices.why: Right: an empty name is the only thing `^$` matches.

prompt: To get a throughput column in MB/s, a benchmark declares how many bytes one round processes with `b.___`.
Match each part of `BenchmarkCount-4  10363  113733 ns/op  16104 B/op  2311 allocs/op` with what it is.
In five runs of unchanged code, which column did not move at all?
hint: It depends only on the code.

choices.why: It moved between 98,755 and 101,532.
Throughput is computed from the time, so it moved with it.
Right: 2311 every time.
It went from 12162 to 10000.

prompt: The candidate cut allocations from 2311 to 2055 per round. By how many?
hint: Two capitalised words in each of 128 repetitions.

prompt: The candidate was measurably faster, by about a tenth. Why did the course still put the old `Count` back?
hint: Measured is not the same as worth keeping.

choices.text: Because the tests failed on the candidate
choices.why: `go test . -count=1` passed on it.

choices.text: Counting was not shown to matter
choices.why: Right: twenty lines, a second path and an in-place write, for a gain nothing needed.

choices.text: Because the two groups of runs overlapped on the axis
choices.why: They did not: 87,509 to 93,811 against 98,755 to 101,532.
They went down by 256.

prompt: Section 02's single run said 113,733 ns/op; five runs a minute later said about 100,000. What does the lesson draw from that?

choices.text: The code got faster on its own
choices.why: Nothing changed; the machine did.

choices.text: The first run is always discarded
choices.why: There is no such rule in the report.
It repeats the measurement; it changes nothing inside it.

choices.text: One run is not a measurement
choices.why: Right. The spread between identical runs is the noise floor.

prompt: `BenchmarkSumN` reported about 150 ns/op and `BenchmarkSumLoop` about 280. What does the disassembly show?
hint: Look for a multiplication in the `sum_test.go:7` lines.

choices.text: That `b.N` loops run on two processors
choices.why: The function's code has nothing to do with processors; one loop has no arithmetic.
Right: the result was unused, so the compiler removed the work and left the counting.

choices.text: That `b.Loop` adds 130 ns of overhead per round
choices.why: The difference is the arithmetic `b.N` lost, not overhead of `b.Loop`.
Its loop is there, inlined; only the body's arithmetic is gone.

prompt: An old benchmark written with `b.N` builds a 1 MB input at the top of the function, then loops. Its numbers seem high. What is missing?
hint: In the `b.N` style, when does the timer start?

choices.why: That adds a throughput column; it does not exclude the setup.
It reports memory; the timing stays the same.
Right. Without it the setup is part of the time; `b.Loop` would exclude it on its own.
Repeating a biased measurement repeats the bias.

prompt: Which habits does the lesson give for a busy machine? Choose all that apply.
hint: Three of them, in a numbered list.

choices.text: Compare runs made one after the other, on the same machine
choices.why: Yes.

choices.text: Look at the spread of several runs before the averages
choices.why: Yes, with `-count`.

choices.text: Compare today's number with one written down last month
choices.why: That is exactly what the first habit warns against.

choices.text: Set GOMAXPROCS to 1 so other programs cannot interfere
choices.why: It limits this program, not the others on the machine.

hint: The course does not install it.

choices.why: There is no such flag.
Right.
`testing` has no statistics tool.
It is not part of the toolchain.

prompt: Put the steps the lesson followed with the candidate `Count` in order.
hint: A faster wrong answer is worth nothing.
items: benchmark the current version several times
benchmark it the same number of times
decide whether the difference is worth the code

prompt: A colleague shows one run where their change made a function 4% faster. Before reading any code, what do you ask for?
hint: How big was the spread between identical runs in this lesson?

choices.why: Memory columns help, but the question is whether 4% is above the noise.

choices.text: The name of the machine it ran on
choices.why: Knowing the machine does not tell you the spread.
A profile says where time goes, not whether 4% is real.
Right. Identical runs here spread by almost 3%, so one run of 4% proves nothing yet.
